analysis.one_liner: Bans large Wall Street investment funds from buying single-family homes and forces them to sell the ones they own.
analysis.headline: The bill to bar large investment funds from buying single-family homes was referred to the House Financial Services Committee in January 2026, where no action has been taken and no other member has signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the Investment Company Act to bar large investment funds — those managing more than $500 million, owning 100 or more single-family homes, or buying more than 5 homes in a 30-day stretch — from purchasing any additional single-family homes [S2]. Funds that already hold homes would have to sell off at least 10% each year until they own none, within 10 years [S2]. The idea is to reduce competition between big institutional investors and ordinary families trying to buy a home [S1, S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary families trying to buy their first or next home would benefit most: with large funds barred from bidding, they would face fewer all-cash institutional competitors in the market, which in many hot markets means less upward pressure on prices [S2]. Individual buyers and smaller local landlords would have more homes available to them [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary families trying to buy homes

how_it_helps.text: It bans covered funds — large investment companies, REITs, and private funds — from buying single-family homes after a 90-day phase-in.
It requires funds that already own single-family homes to divest at least 10% per year until they hold none, within 10 years.
By shrinking competition in the buyer pool, it aims to make it easier for ordinary families to purchase homes.

analysis.who_pays: Large private funds, REITs, and investment companies that buy and rent single-family homes would bear the cost: they would lose a growing business line and would have to sell off existing holdings over a decade [S2]. Some renters in fund-owned homes could see their landlords change during the sell-off [S2].
analysis.who_pays_short: Large investment funds owning rental homes

drawbacks.text: Existing funds get 10 years to fully divest, selling off at least 10% per year, which delays any effect on prices for years and could let investors time their sales for maximum value.

The definition of a covered fund only reaches funds with over $500 million in assets, funds owning 100 or more homes, or funds that bought more than 5 homes in 30 days — leaving many smaller but still significant corporate landlords outside the restriction.

A mandate to sell large numbers of homes over a decade could reduce rental supply in some markets or affect property values in neighborhoods with many fund-owned homes, a cost an honest supporter would need to weigh.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit for prospective homebuyers could be real where institutional buyers have bid up prices, but the costs and design problems are serious: existing corporate owners get a decade-long runway to sell at their own pace, a $500 million or 100-home threshold exempts many mid-size corporate buyers, and homeowners whose neighborhoods have many fund-owned rentals could see prices and rental availability affected if supply is dumped or withheld. The bill never advanced far enough to be amended or tested, so its actual impact cannot be known.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, and nothing has happened since — no hearing, no vote, and no cosponsors.

narrative.text: Rep. Luna introduced the bill on January 22, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The action history shows no committee consideration, no markup, no floor vote, and no further action after the referral.
No other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large investment funds and institutional landlords are better off for now, since nothing has interfered with their ability to buy and hold single-family homes.

for.name: Rep. Anna Paulina Luna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: With no cosponsors, no committee action, and no votes, the record shows no pattern of support or opposition from either party.

industries.industry: Institutional single-family rental owners (large private funds, REITs, investment companies)
industries.note: The bill blocks large funds from buying more single-family homes and forces a 10-year phased sell-off of homes they already own, threatening a business model built on converting owner-occupied housing into rentals.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized landlords and homebuilders
industries.note: Smaller buyers under the asset and ownership thresholds are not covered and could face less competition for acquisitions; homebuilders could lose a large bulk-purchase customer.
Buyers could face less competition from all-cash institutional offers, but some renters in fund-owned homes could see ownership change during forced divestment, and the effects would vary by market.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Financial Services Committee with zero cosponsors and no scheduled action; most bills in this position never receive a markup or a floor vote, so its likely path is to die quietly at the end of the Congress unless the sponsor builds support or leadership decides to prioritize it.
